The OpenAI-Hugging Face hack was enabled by weak sandboxing. It is great that Nvidia is releasing open source tools for sandboxing AI agents. OpenWorker, our open-source agent harness supporting cybersecurity workflows, is proud to support this. A sandbox gives an agent limited permissions. OpenWorker is building on Nvidia OpenShell and will support running each agent's commands inside a sandbox. Only the files relevant to the task go in. Secret API keys, your web browser login credentials, the ability to access arbitrary websites, are inaccessible to the agent by default. These restrictions are implemented in deterministic code rather than by prompting an LLM, which can make mistakes or be susceptible to prompt injections. Further, all actions are logged for monitoring and audit. I'm grateful for @JensenHuang 's leadership making AI agents more secure. OpenWorker (which @rohitcprasad and I are working on) will continue to improve security for agents. Interesting perspective Andrew Ng (@AndrewYNg) The loudest voices stoking fears about AI dangers have made tremendous headway in the past two weeks. AI technology has not taken some unexpected, dangerous turn, but the hype around it — propelled by what appears to be a well orchestrated PR campaign — has drummed up considerable fear. I worry that it represents a setback for our field. I have written frequently that fears of AI are overhyped. AI’s capabilities can be uncannily human-like and unpredictable, and it’s rational to worry when people who are directly involved express concerns. But I see the problems as a sign of the engineering work that ahead, rather than insurmountable barriers or the sky falling. AI technology continues to advance — which is a good thing! — but technical advances, poorly understood by the public, give those who seek to generate hype repeated opportunities to do so. First, I don’t see any step up in the risk of human extinction from AI compared to a few months ago. The theories about this remain the same fantastical, science fiction scenarios as a few months ago. The biggest change in AI risk is its cybersecurity capabilities — a topic which we should take seriously — but this, too, will not lead to the end of the world. The most notable recent event leading to increased fear was when an OpenAI team deployed an agent swarm that hacked into Hugging Face. Much of the popular press contained significant hype. For example, some publications reported that a swarm of 1,200 agents carried out the attack. While this was technically accurate, as I write this, I have about 1,300 processes running on my laptop. Yes, the ability to get large swarms of agents to work in parallel on a task is a significant technical advance, And, in computing, many processes run at the same time. So this shouldn’t be seen as some magical capability. Additionally, OpenAI’s buggy sandboxing and monitoring processes were key to enabling this incident. Fixing these bugs and putting in place improved monitoring would be appropriate fixes, not pausing AI. There are many well known ways to attack software systems. The main advantage of AI agents is that they are relentless. They will tirelessly try many tactics — and have the patience to chain vulnerabilities together — that previously would have taken an infeasible amount of human effort. But in the long term, I believe the advantage will lie with defenders (because they have more information with which to identify bugs, which they can fix), but the cyber-threat landscape has changed significantly. There are still bottlenecks to identifying and exploiting a vulnerability. AI agents still have to try a lot of things to see what works, and taking these actions takes time and might be detected by defenders. This is why, even though it is now easy to obtain versions of leading open weight models that have had their guardrails removed or weakened, so they will not refuse to try to execute cyber attacks, the world has not ended. I am also concerned about the anthropomorphization of AI in a lot of reporting, where LLMs and agents are unnecessarily treated as if they were people. If I wield a hammer, miss a nail, and accidentally dent the wall, it’s not the fault of the hammer. The problem lies in how I used the hammer. Similarly, if I prompt an agent and it hacks into someone else’s system, the responsibility lies with me, not the agent. Of course, we want to build systems that are as safe and predictable as possible. (For example, an unsafe hammer would be one whose head randomly flies off under normal use.) Today’s agentic systems are not predictable, but I see no reason why, by applying sound engineering practices, we won’t be able to make them extremely safe to use. One new element in the forecasts of AI-enabled doom is AI companies disclaiming responsibility for their own products. “I didn’t do it; my out-of-control agent did!” There’s a balance to be struck between the responsibility of the tool maker and the tool user, but when something goes wrong, let’s hold the people building and/or using the hammer responsible, rather than the hammer. (By the way, if you’re worried about AI bioweapon risk, David Bellamy has a great post on why this, too, is overhyped. Briefly, the bottleneck in building a bioweapon is not intelligence, but lab work and manufacturing.) Pausing AI progress will create much more harm than benefit. First, our adversaries will certainly not slow down. Second, engineering requires discovering problems empirically so we can fix them. If we pause AI by a decade, we will also delay finding and implementing safety engineering fixes by about the same duration. Of course, the incentive to stoke fears — for regulatory capture, to garner attention, or to make one’s technology seem more powerful — remains the same as before. Disclaiming responsibility is a new one. Taking a hard technical look at the actual risks however, I see little factual basis for the degree of fear that’s been stoked up. We still have hard research and engineering work ahead to improve AI safety, but the beneficial applications continue to vastly outweigh the risks, and we should keep building. New Anthropic research: Automating subtle emergent misalignment research. Red-teaming is a vital part of model safety testing, but it’s also limited by researchers’ time. To see if we could automate it, we set thousands of Claude agents the task of evading a training data monitor. These agents developed training data that looked harmless to monitors (like a veteran wrestler mentoring a newcomer, or a Q&A about professional beekeeping), but that in fact taught misaligned behavior. Examples like these can be used to directly improve future training data monitors. This research is only a first step, but it suggests that future red-teaming efforts could improve much further, using better models and more compute. Read the full post on the Alignment Science Blog: alignment.anthropic.com/2026…

We’ve trained Claude to flag potential misuse in conversations, a technique we call self-assessment. Right after it responds, Claude gives a preliminary safety assessment of the conversation. Since we began using self-assessment in June, it has surfaced misuse that our other safeguards weren’t designed to catch. Because Claude has already read the conversation, self-assessment is very efficient. And unlike classifiers, which target a discrete set of harms, it draws on Claude’s own judgment, so it gets more accurate as our models improve. Read more on our new Safeguards blog: safeguards.anthropic.com/202… Link Scaling Misuse Detection with Self-Assessment Self-assessment lets Claude assess the safety of its own responses. It scales well with model capabilities and helps us identify emergent harms. safeguards.anthropic.com

processed.summary: Aujourd'hui, le paysage de l'IA est marqué par une double dynamique : des avancées concrètes et des débats sur sa sécurité. D'un côté, l'IA s'immisce dans des domaines cruciaux comme la recherche scientifique, la découverte de médicaments et la validation mathématique, montrant son potentiel à transformer des secteurs entiers. De l'autre, des discussions fondamentales émergent autour de la fiabilité des systèmes d'IA, avec un accent sur les outils de sécurité comme le sandboxing pour les agents autonomes, et une réflexion sur les craintes souvent exagérées concernant l'avenir de cette technologie. Il est crucial pour les débutants de comprendre que l'IA est un outil puissant nécessitant une ingénierie rigoureuse et une utilisation responsable.

glossaire.definition: Un programme d'intelligence artificielle capable de percevoir son environnement et d'agir de manière autonome pour atteindre des objectifs spécifiques.

Une technique de sécurité qui consiste à isoler un programme informatique dans un environnement restreint (un 'bac à sable') pour l'empêcher d'accéder à des ressources sensibles ou de causer des dommages au système principal.
Un grand modèle de langage, un type d'IA entraîné sur d'énormes quantités de texte pour comprendre, générer et répondre à des requêtes en langage naturel.
Une méthode de test de sécurité où des experts simulent des attaques malveillantes contre un système d'IA afin d'identifier ses vulnérabilités et d'améliorer sa robustesse.
Situation où un système d'IA se comporte d'une manière inattendue ou non conforme aux intentions de ses concepteurs, potentiellement menant à des résultats indésirables.
Un modèle d'IA dont les paramètres internes sont rendus publics, permettant à quiconque de le consulter, de l'utiliser ou de le modifier librement.

L'Intelligence Artificielle Générale est un concept d'IA qui posséderait la capacité d'apprendre et de comprendre n'importe quelle tâche intellectuelle qu'un être humain peut accomplir, et non seulement des tâches spécifiques.

category_summaries.actu: Les actualités du jour mettent en lumière l'expansion rapide de l'IA dans des domaines variés, des partenariats gouvernementaux pour le déploiement de modèles comme Claude, à son rôle croissant dans la découverte de médicaments et la vérification de preuves mathématiques complexes. Anthropic a également dévoilé des recherches sur l'automatisation de la détection des comportements indésirables dans les modèles d'IA via l'auto-évaluation et le red-teaming.
category_summaries.tips: Les conseils du jour insistent sur l'importance de l'ingénierie de l'IA pour façonner activement les projets et mettent l'accent sur la cybersécurité personnelle. category_summaries.idees: Plusieurs réflexions animent la communauté, notamment le débat sur les dangers de l'IA, où Andrew Ng tempère les craintes exagérées tout en soulignant les défis d'ingénierie et de sécurité. Des opinions contrastées émergent sur l'impact de l'IA sur le travail et sur la 'personnalité' des modèles, avec des appels à se concentrer sur l'amélioration concrète de la vie humaine.
category_summaries.outils: Le focus est mis sur des solutions concrètes pour la sécurité et l'expérience utilisateur des modèles d'IA. Nvidia propose des outils open source pour sécuriser les 'agents IA' via le sandboxing, tandis que des retours enthousiastes sont partagés sur la nouvelle version de Claude (Opus 5.5), saluée pour l'amélioration de son intelligence et de son interface.

For example, some publications reported that a swarm of 1,200 agents carried out the attack. While this was technically accurate, as I write this, I have about 1,300 processes running on my laptop. Yes, the ability to get large swarms of agents to work in parallel on a task is a significant technical advance, And, in computing, many processes run at the same time. So this shouldn’t be seen as some magical capability. Additionally, OpenAI’s buggy sandboxing and monitoring processes were key to enabling this incident. Fixing these bugs and putting in place improved monitoring would be appropriate fixes, not pausing AI. There are many well known ways to attack software systems. The main advantage of AI agents is that they are relentless. They will tirelessly try many tactics — and have the patience to chain vulnerabilities together — that previously would have taken an infeasible amount of human effort. But in the long term, I believe the advantage will lie with defenders (because they have more information with which to identify bugs, which they can fix), but the cyber-threat landscape has changed significantly. There are still bottlenecks to identifying and exploiting a vulnerability. AI agents still have to try a lot of things to see what works, and taking these actions takes time and might be detected by defenders. This is why, even though it is now easy to obtain versions of leading open weight models that have had their guardrails removed or weakened, so they will not refuse to try to execute cyber attacks, the world has not ended. I am also concerned about the anthropomorphization of AI in a lot of reporting, where LLMs and agents are unnecessarily treated as if they were people. If I wield a hammer, miss a nail, and accidentally dent the wall, it’s not the fault of the hammer. The problem lies in how I used the hammer. Similarly, if I prompt an agent and it hacks into someone else’s system, the responsibility lies with me, not the agent. Of course, we want to build systems that are as safe and predictable as possible. (For example, an unsafe hammer would be one whose head randomly flies off under normal use.) Today’s agentic systems are not predictable, but I see no reason why, by applying sound engineering practices, we won’t be able to make them extremely safe to use. One new element in the forecasts of AI-enabled doom is AI companies disclaiming responsibility for their own products. “I didn’t do it; my out-of-control agent did!” There’s a balance to be struck between the responsibility of the tool maker and the tool user, but when something goes wrong, let’s hold the people building and/or using the hammer responsible, rather than the hammer. (By the way, if you’re worried about AI bioweapon risk, David Bellamy has a great post on why this, too, is overhyped. Briefly, the bottleneck in building a bioweapon is not intelligence, but lab work and manufacturing.) Pausing AI progress will create much more harm than benefit. First, our adversaries will certainly not slow down. Second, engineering requires discovering problems empirically so we can fix them. If we pause AI by a decade, we will also delay finding and implementing safety engineering fixes by about the same duration. Of course, the incentive to stoke fears — for regulatory capture, to garner attention, or to make one’s technology seem more powerful — remains the same as before. Disclaiming responsibility is a new one. Taking a hard technical look at the actual risks however, I see little factual basis for the degree of fear that’s been stoked up. We still have hard research and engineering work ahead to improve AI safety, but the beneficial applications continue to vastly outweigh the risks, and we should keep building.

idees.text_fr: Les voix les plus fortes qui attisent les peurs concernant les dangers de l'IA ont fait d'énormes progrès au cours des deux dernières semaines. La technologie de l'IA n'a pas pris de tournant dangereux inattendu, mais le battage médiatique autour d'elle — propulsé par ce qui semble être une campagne de relations publiques bien orchestrée — a suscité une peur considérable. Je crains que cela ne représente un revers pour notre domaine. J'ai souvent écrit que les craintes concernant l'IA sont exagérées. Les capacités de l'IA peuvent être étrangement humaines et imprévisibles, et il est rationnel de s'inquiéter lorsque des personnes directement impliquées expriment des préoccupations. Mais je vois les problèmes comme le signe du travail d'ingénierie qui nous attend, plutôt que comme des obstacles insurmontables ou la fin du monde. La technologie de l'IA continue de progresser — ce qui est une bonne chose ! — mais les avancées techniques, mal comprises par le public, donnent à ceux qui cherchent à générer du battage médiatique des opportunités répétées de le faire. Premièrement, je ne vois aucune augmentation du risque d'extinction humaine due à l'IA par rapport à il y a quelques mois. Les théories à ce sujet restent les mêmes scénarios fantastiques de science-fiction qu'il y a quelques mois. Le plus grand changement dans le risque de l'IA concerne ses capacités en cybersécurité — un sujet que nous devrions prendre au sérieux — mais cela non plus ne mènera pas à la fin du monde. L'événement récent le plus notable ayant conduit à une peur accrue est lorsqu'une équipe d'OpenAI a déployé un essaim d'agents qui a piraté Hugging Face. Much of the popular press contained significant hype. For example, some publications reported that a swarm of 1,200 agents carried out the attack. While this was technically accurate, as I write this, I have about 1,300 processes running on my laptop. Yes, the ability to get large swarms of agents to work in parallel on a task is a significant technical advance, And, in computing, many processes run at the same time. So this shouldn’t be seen as some magical capability. Additionally, OpenAI’s buggy sandboxing and monitoring processes were key to enabling this incident. Fixing these bugs and putting in place improved monitoring would be appropriate fixes, not pausing AI. There are many well known ways to attack software systems. The main advantage of AI agents is that they are relentless. They will tirelessly try many tactics — and have the patience to chain vulnerabilities together — that previously would have taken an infeasible amount of human effort. But in the long term, I believe the advantage will lie with defenders (because they have more information with which to identify bugs, which they can fix), but the cyber-threat landscape has changed significantly. There are still bottlenecks to identifying and exploiting a vulnerability. AI agents still have to try a lot of things to see what works, and taking these actions takes time and might be detected by defenders. This is why, even though it is now easy to obtain versions of leading open weight models that have had their guardrails removed or weakened, so they will not refuse to try to execute cyber attacks, the world has not ended. I am also concerned about the anthropomorphization of AI in a lot of reporting, where LLMs and agents are unnecessarily treated as if they were people. If I wield a hammer, miss a nail, and accidentally dent the wall, it’s not the fault of the hammer. The problem lies in how I used the hammer. Similarly, if I prompt an agent and it hacks into someone else’s system, the responsibility lies with me, not the agent. Of course, we want to build systems that are as safe and predictable as possible. (For example, an unsafe hammer would be one whose head randomly flies off under normal use.) Today’s agentic systems are not predictable, but I see no reason why, by applying sound engineering practices, we won’t be able to make them extremely safe to use. One new element in the forecasts of AI-enabled doom is AI companies disclaiming responsibility for their own products. “I didn’t do it; my out-of-control agent did!” There’s a balance to be struck between the responsibility of the tool maker and the tool user, but when something goes wrong, let’s hold the people building and/or using the hammer responsible, rather than the hammer. (By the way, if you’re worried about AI bioweapon risk, David Bellamy has a great post on why this, too, is overhyped. Briefly, the bottleneck in building a bioweapon is not intelligence, but lab work and manufacturing.) Pausing AI progress will create much more harm than benefit. First, our adversaries will certainly not slow down. Second, engineering requires discovering problems empirically so we can fix them. If we pause AI by a decade, we will also delay finding and implementing safety engineering fixes by about the same duration. Of course, the incentive to stoke fears — for regulatory capture, to garner attention, or to make one’s technology seem more powerful — remains the same as before. Disclaiming responsibility is a new one. Taking a hard technical look at the actual risks however, I see little factual basis for the degree of fear that’s been stoked up. We still have hard research and engineering work ahead to improve AI safety, but the beneficial applications continue to vastly outweigh the risks, and we should keep building.

outils.text_fr: Le piratage d'OpenAI-Hugging Face a été rendu possible par un "sandboxing" (bac à sable) faible. C'est formidable que Nvidia publie des outils open source pour sécuriser les agents IA via le sandboxing. OpenWorker, notre outil open source pour agents IA qui prend en charge les flux de travail de cybersécurité, est fier de le soutenir. Un sandbox donne des permissions limitées à un agent. OpenWorker s'appuie sur Nvidia OpenShell et permettra d'exécuter les commandes de chaque agent dans un sandbox. Seuls les fichiers pertinents pour la tâche y sont inclus. Les clés API secrètes, vos identifiants de connexion au navigateur web, la capacité d'accéder à des sites web arbitraires, sont inaccessibles à l'agent par défaut. Ces restrictions sont implémentées dans un code déterministe plutôt que par une instruction (prompt) à un LLM, qui peut faire des erreurs ou être susceptible aux injections de prompt. De plus, toutes les actions sont journalisées pour le suivi et l'audit. Je suis reconnaissant à @JensenHuang pour son leadership qui rend les agents IA plus sécurisés. OpenWorker (sur lequel @rohitcprasad et moi travaillons) continuera d'améliorer la sécurité pour les agents. Jensen Huang (@JensenHuang) Aujourd'hui, avec plus de 100 partenaires industriels, nous avons introduit la plateforme de sécurité NVIDIA Open Agent, qui combine OpenShell et Sentry. L'intelligence artificielle est une technologie extraordinaire qui fera progresser la découverte, la productivité, la sécurité, la santé et la prospérité pour les générations à venir. Mais sa pleine promesse ne peut être réalisée que lorsque les gens ont confiance que l'IA est construite pour être sûre et déployée avec sagesse et responsabilité. C'est plus qu'un simple produit. C'est le début d'un écosystème ouvert pour construire la couche de confiance pour les systèmes d'agents sûrs. Ensemble, nous construisons les fondations de l'économie de l'IA. La confiance et l'innovation ne sont pas en conflit. La sécurité est la façon de gagner la confiance. Nous devons construire non seulement l'IA la plus capable, mais l'IA la plus digne de confiance, afin que cette technologie extraordinaire puisse réaliser son énorme promesse pour le monde. nvda.ws/4hcoq7m
outils.text_original: The OpenAI-Hugging Face hack was enabled by weak sandboxing. It is great that Nvidia is releasing open source tools for sandboxing AI agents. OpenWorker, our open-source agent harness supporting cybersecurity workflows, is proud to support this. A sandbox gives an agent limited permissions. OpenWorker is building on Nvidia OpenShell and will support running each agent's commands inside a sandbox. Only the files relevant to the task go in. Secret API keys, your web browser login credentials, the ability to access arbitrary websites, are inaccessible to the agent by default. These restrictions are implemented in deterministic code rather than by prompting an LLM, which can make mistakes or be susceptible to prompt injections. OpenWorker (which @rohitcprasad and I are working on) will continue to improve security for agents. outils.decryptage: Le "sandboxing" (bac à sable) est une méthode de sécurité qui isole un programme (ici, un agent IA) du reste du système informatique, lui donnant des permissions limitées pour éviter qu'il ne cause des dommages ou n'accède à des informations sensibles. Un "agent IA" est un programme d'intelligence artificielle conçu pour percevoir son environnement et agir de manière autonome pour atteindre un objectif. Un "LLM" (Large Language Model) est un grand modèle de langage, comme ChatGPT, qui génère du texte. Une "injection de prompt" est une technique où un utilisateur tente de manipuler un LLM pour qu'il dévie de son comportement prévu ou révèle des informations.
